$comment: What the mock Merchant sells. `cmd/merchant -catalogue` reads it, and a fifth product is an
edit here rather than a source change, a pull request and a review.
Nothing above this file was ever the obstacle. `item.attr.<name>` is open by construction —
AGENTS.md: 'core does not know what a flight is and should not have to' — the field registry
names nothing aviation, and Catalogue.Search evaluates constraints against a subject without
knowing what it is selling. Four Go literals were the whole of what stood in the way.
The rules are in merchant.CatalogueFile.Validate and nowhere else. There is deliberately no
JSON Schema beside this file: contracts/ is a model generator, every schema there becomes a Go
type and a TypeScript type, and a catalogue is instances — so `make generate` would emit a type
per product. A schema written here instead, purely to validate, would state the loader's rules
a second time, and the second copy is the one that drifts.
`currency` is one field for the whole file. Per-offer currency would let a `lte 40000 USD` cap
sit against a `38000 EUR` price, and constraint's money comparison refuses a mismatch rather
than converting — so the symptom is not a wrong answer but a prompt that matches nothing, with
no failing test anywhere. Amounts are minor units: 24000 is $240.00.
`merchant` carries no identifier. Who this merchant is has to agree with cmd/merchant, which is
given it on the command line, so a value written here could only ever drift from the binary it
names — the same reason deploy/demo.json does not restate the four role identifiers. 5399 is
miscellaneous general merchandise, which is what a shop selling flights, bicycles, concert
tickets and ladders from one counter would trade under.
The offer carrying `route.origin` and `route.destination` is the flight, and the inventory the
Human Present flow buys through — GET /checkout?from=BEG&to=PMI — quotes that route on that
offer's own prices. Exactly one offer may carry them; none and two are both refused at load.
The rule is the attributes rather than the category, because 'flights' is a string whoever
wrote this file picked, while those two attribute names are already load-bearing: the scripted
prompt that goes looking for the flight constrains on both by name.
`scenario` is the offer declaring what it is for, and it is the part of this file that is not
obvious. `cap` is the bound the prompt going looking for this offer places on the price; `found`
is what that prompt is then supposed to do — `always`, `at-the-last-price`, or `never` for
something the search is meant not to return. Those are the same claims a Go table makes about
these four products, one row each, and holding them here is what makes a fifth product state
one too. A price edited past its cap does not fail to compile, does not fail to load, and would
not fail a test written against four constants a new product never acquires: it produces a
search box that answers nothing for a prompt the documentation says works.
`image_url` is root-relative and refused at load if it is not, including a protocol-relative
`//host/…`. That argument is older than this file — an image fetched from a host this project
does not control would make a screenshot depend on somebody else's uptime, and would put a
network call one careless test away — but it used to be a comment beside a literal a reviewer
had read. The guard exists because the data moved: an editor is now enough to change it.
Every offer moves at least once. Issue #192 is why it started that way and issue #198 is why
only two of them still need to: a Human Not Present watch attempts on a step change and never on
a price — see agent.Watch — so the concert and the ladders, which hold one flat price already
inside their own cap, gave a watch nothing to act on and ran until the open mandate pair's hour
expired, a state about the clock rather than about the purchase.
#198 answered that one level up. Those two prompts carry no condition — "two tickets, up to $160
all in" and "find and buy telescopic ladders, cheapest" are instructions — so the interpreter
now says so, and the agent buys at the opening price rather than waiting for a step. **Their
second price is therefore no longer load-bearing.** It is kept rather than removed, because it is
what a browser started before this frontend learnt to send the trigger still needs, and because
prices four tests and every screenshot are written against are not worth moving to delete a fact
nothing now depends on. Removing them is a decision on its own terms, not a tidy-up.
The four still fall into two pairs, and what tells them apart is now *what the sentence asked*
rather than why the price moves. The flight and the bicycle are conditional — they open outside
the cap their own prompt names and step into it, which is the beat the autonomous flow exists to
show. The concert and the ladders are instructions, and were never outside their cap: nothing is
ever refused on either, and the purchase completes at the first price the merchant quotes. A
screen where all four crossed into range at once would still be one story told four times — this
keeps it two.
The bicycle's and the concert's identifiers are named character for character by the scripted
constraint sets in internal/agent/interpret/scenarios.go, because those prompts approve one
specific object rather than a class of object. Nothing enforces the match — core-isolation keeps
that package and the merchant from sharing a table — and the symptom of a divergence is not a
failing test but a demo where the prompt finds nothing. Grep for the identifier before changing
either side. The flight and the ladders are matched on attributes and category instead.
